add.term: routes to an accurate self-report (introspection, self-simulation, post-hoc rationalization)
add.quote: However, a self-report can be accurate without being introspective. An accurate report may be caused by truly accessing the internal state (introspection), by the model recomputing that state in a new context (self-simulation), or by exploiting information that merely correlates with its internals (post-hoc rationalization), a route also known in LLMs as causal bypassing.
add.gloss: Three causal routes to an accurate self-report; §1 extends the cited introspection/rationalization distinction with self-simulation. Accuracy alone cannot tell the routes apart.

add.quote: However, an accurate self-report can arise from three routes: (i) introspection, the report is caused by the target internal state itself;
add.gloss: A self-report is introspective when the internal state it describes causes it; carries to LLMs the causal-route criterion the same paragraph attributes to Nisbett & Wilson.

add.quote: (ii) self-simulation, the model recomputes that state in a new context (using its own weights, the source model is privileged relative to other models, even without reading the original internals);
add.gloss: Privileged but non-introspective route: the model recomputes the state with its own weights in a new context; the paper's tests cannot separate it from introspection.

add.quote: Lindsey (2025) unified them, arguing that an LLM self-report must be: accurate (correctly describing the internal state), grounded (causally dependent
add.gloss: Four conditions: accurate, grounded (causally dependent on the internal state), internal (not inferred from prior sampled outputs), metacognitive (based on a representation formed before or during the report).

add.quote: If Mj successfully predicts yi (on par with Mbase ) only from xi despite having entirely distinct weights from Mbase , it suggests that the task does not strictly require privileged self-access to be accomplished.
add.gloss: External LLMs trained (ICL/LoRA) on the same input-label pairs; matching self-accuracy shows the rationalization route is available, so self-accuracy is no evidence of privileged access.

add.quote: Static-Embedding Baselines (fj ∈ F): We train simple, non-autoregressive classifiers (e.g., Logistic Regression, SVM) to predict yi using only static sentence embeddings of xi . High baseline accuracy (fj (xi ) ≈ yi ) strongly suggests causal bypassing.
add.gloss: Classifiers on frozen sentence embeddings of the input alone predict the self-report label; high accuracy means surface text suffices, which the paper reads as causal bypassing.

add.quote: we plot the source’s own LoRA reporter accuracy minus the mean accuracy of the three other LLM reporters on the same rows, in percentage points, averaged over 3 seeds. Positive values mean the model predicts its own labels better than other models do.
add.gloss: Self-reporter accuracy minus mean accuracy of other LLM reporters on the same source's behaviour-derived labels; a positive residual is the only candidate evidence of a privileged route.

add.quote: Self advantage after removing reporter skill and source difficulty, all 15 datasets (LoRA, three seeds 42/92/142). For each dataset an additive model acc[r, s] = ar + bs is fit on the cross cells only and used to predict the self cell; the entry is the actual self accuracy minus that prediction, in points of accuracy.
add.gloss: Self accuracy minus an additive reporter-skill plus source-predictability prediction fitted on cross cells; the residual is compatible with introspection, self-simulation or familiarity with own weights.

add.quote: Second, given that most existing evaluations are focused on single tasks, it remains unclear whether success is attributable to a general introspective capability or to a task-specific route. Here, our cross-task transfer test distinguishes the two because a route built on task-specific shortcuts does not generalize across other introspection tasks.
add.gloss: Fine-tuning gains that fail to transfer to other introspection task families mark a task-specific shortcut route; §6 adds that transfer alone would not prove privileged access.

add.quote: Self-Prediction (Binder et al., 2025): The model predicts elements of its exact future generation sequence y = {y1 , y2 , ..., yT } (e.g., the first token y1 ) prior to standard autoregressive decoding.
add.gloss: Self-report task: the model predicts properties of its own upcoming output (first character or word, chosen option, ethical stance), scored by exact match against its actual behaviour.

add.quote: Confidence Reporting (Cencerrado et al., 2025): The model estimates the correctness of its hypothetical answer to a given query via a binary classification c ∈ {0, 1}.
add.gloss: Self-report task: the model says True/False whether its own answer to the question would be correct; App. B.4 finds static text baselines largely solve it.

set.quote: (iii) rationalization, the report is caused by information that merely correlates with the state that any capable reporter can exploit. The latter, also known as causal bypassing (Morris & Plunkett, 2025), is the natural null hypothesis for introspection claims.
set.gloss: Accurate self-report caused by information merely correlated with the internal state, which any capable reporter could exploit; also called causal bypassing; the null hypothesis for introspection claims.

fix.reason: The abstract passage states all three routes and cites nobody; the §1 passage is the explicit definition and the one citing Morris & Plunkett. The abstract passage moves to a new taxonomy row.

papers.note: Added the three-route taxonomy and its introspection and self-simulation categories, Lindsey's criteria, the cross-model and static-baseline tests, two self-advantage metrics, the transfer criterion and two self-report tasks. Steering awareness and activation monitoring were left out because they detect internal states.
Full text adds nothing: §1's 'faithful and transparent' symbolic engines is the notion row #2 already holds. Faithfulness is never measured; §4.1 reads accuracy gains as faithfulness gains.

add.quote: Plausibility via Vera (Liu et al., 2023a): Vera is a trained commonsense statement verification T5-11B model, that provides a numerical score between $0$ and $1$ , indicating the plausibility of declarative sentences. | | $\textsc{Plausibility}(\hat{R})\ =\textsc{Vera}(\hat{R})$ | | (1)
add.gloss: Rationale plausibility is the 0-1 score that the Vera commonsense statement verifier (T5-11B) assigns to the generated rationale; used as a training reward and automatic metric.

add.quote: For each instance, we ask three distinct annotators from a pool of qualified annotators to compare the two rationales across three settings, for a given question and correct answer pair: Plausibility and Consistency, which are defined in the same manner as the rewards, and an overall Preference rating.
add.gloss: Three annotators compare two rationales for a question and its correct answer on plausibility, consistency and preference; scored as the share of items where the majority prefers each system.

add.quote: Some recent works on other necessary rationale properties are REV Chen et al. (2023a) (novelty of information, faithfulness towards the predicted label), ROSCOE Golovneva et al. (2022) / ReCEval Prasad et al. (2023) (score steps of reasoning), LAS Hase et al. (2020) (faithfulness towards predicted labels) etc.
add.gloss: Calls faithfulness to the model's predicted label, as measured by REV and LAS, a further necessary rationale property. The paper's own consistency instead targets the gold label.

add.quote: Therefore, we note that selecting strong rewards, as well as careful qualitative investigation is extremely important to prevent this kind of reward hacking – where an increase in individual numerical reward scores do not guarantee overall qualitative improvements.
add.gloss: Reward scores rise while rationales get worse, e.g. repetitive text under a factuality reward and incomplete rationales under factuality plus diversity (Table 4).

set.quote: Wiegreffe et al. (2021) provide a framework to evaluate the association between a rationale and a label with the help of two reference LMs that are trained to predict the answer with ( $\mathbb{M_{QR}}$ ) and without ( $\mathbb{M_{Q}}$ ) the rationale in the input. More formally, | | $\textsc{Consistency}(\hat{R})=P_{\mathbb{M_{QR}}}(O|Q,\hat{R})-P_{\mathbb{M_{Q}}}(O|Q)$ | | (2) Consistency is a numerical score between $-1$ and $1$ that indicates the faithfulness of the rationale towards the gold answer, like the implementation by Wiegreffe et al. (2021).
set.gloss: Per-instance gain in gold-answer probability when two reference T5 LMs see the rationale (Eq. 2); the paper calls it the rationale's faithfulness towards the gold answer.

fix.reason: Quote omitted the operative Eq. 2. Stance: Wiegreffe et al. 2021 score rationale quality as a dataset-level accuracy difference (IR→O minus I→O). This paper changes it to a per-instance probability difference, uses it as a reward and renames it consistency, so the row is adapted.

papers.note: Added the Vera plausibility metric, the human pairwise plausibility and consistency judgments, the §5.1 faithfulness-to-predicted-label property (REV, LAS) and the §5.2 reward-hacking failure mode. Fixed row #3 to include Eq. 2 and set its stance to adapted.
